IN.text: UPI handled 85.5% of all payments by number in the second half of 2025, but only about 9.5% by value: it is how people pay for everyday, small things.
Household debt reached 41.3% of GDP by March 2025, led by consumption loans: many people buy big items on loans and EMIs.
Households' net financial saving was 7.0% of national disposable income in 2024-25, up from 5.8% a year earlier.

US.text: In 2024, credit cards were used for 35% of payments, debit cards for 30% and cash for 14%; credit card use keeps growing.
23% of purchases and person-to-person payments were made remotely (online or by phone) in 2024, a share that has risen every year since 2021.
The personal saving rate fell to 3.8% of disposable income in September 2026, a near four-year low: most income is spent.

UK.text: Card payments were 64% of all UK payments in 2025, and debit cards alone more than half; contactless and phone wallets are everyday habits.
Cash fell below 10% of UK payments for the first time in 2024.

EU.text: In the euro area, cash was still used for 52% of in-store payments in 2024 (59% in 2022), mostly for small amounts; cards lead for payments over 50 euros.
62% of euro area consumers said it is important to keep cash as a way to pay.
Euro area households saved 14.4% of their disposable income in the last quarter of 2025.

CN.text: Mobile wallets such as Alipay and WeChat Pay made up about 89% of in-store spending in 2025, as reported by Caixin; cards are rarely used.
Disposable income per person was 43,377 yuan in 2025 nationwide and 56,502 yuan for urban residents.
Household bank deposits grew nearly 10% in 2025 while borrowing weakened: people are saving cautiously.

JP.text: Cashless payments were 58.0% of consumer spending in 2025, up from 16.6% in 2010; cash is still common.
Credit cards make up most of Japan's cashless payments.

biases.loss aversion: Losing money hurts you more than saving the same amount pleases you, so you worry about paying for something that turns out bad.
biases.anchoring: You judge a price against the first price you saw for something similar.
biases.social proof: You trust what friends and other buyers do more than what a brand says about itself.
biases.status quo: You stick with what you already use unless the new option is clearly better.
biases.present bias: Today's cost feels bigger to you than benefits that come later.
biases.price means quality: You assume cheap means low quality and a higher price means better.
biases.mental budget: You keep a rough budget for each kind of spending and dislike going over it.
biases.free is powerful: Anything free (a trial, a sample, a free extra) feels worth more to you than it really is.
biases.authority: You give weight to experts, reviews by professionals and well-known names.
biases.choice overload: When there are many options or details, you put off deciding.

checks: the total cost, including delivery, fees, taxes or add-ons
how you would pay (and whether your usual way of paying works)
when and how you would get it, and how much effort that takes
what happens if it is late, broken or not as described: returns, refunds, cancelling
warranty, support, and who you would call or message
who is behind it and whether they will still be around
what data they collect and what they do with it
how much of your time it takes to start using it
b2b_checks: the total cost over a year, including installation, setup, training, maintenance and renewals
the return on the money: what it saves or earns the business, and how fast
who else has to approve it, and whether you can justify it to them
contract terms: minimum period, lock-in, cancelling, payment terms and a proper GST/VAT invoice
support: response times, on-site service, maintenance contract (AMC), warranty and spares
how it fits what the business already uses, and the cost and risk of switching
proof it works: references, case studies, clients like you
whether the supplier is reliable and will still be around
